idiom_name: type Expr interface { Eval(*Context) (Value, error) } implemented by one struct per rule
implementation_notes: Go expresses the classic structure directly: a one-method interface is the AbstractExpression role, a struct per grammar rule implements it, and a context struct carries bindings. The standard library's go/ast shows the same node-set-with-methods shape, and ast.Walk / ast.Inspect are the idiomatic way to add operations that must stay outside the node types. The method form is the right default: it keeps each rule's semantics with its data and lets a new node type arrive without touching existing code.
pitfalls: Calling Eval on a nil interface panics: return errors for unknown nodes and variables rather than reaching for panic.
Boxing a value receiver into the interface allocates; pick pointer or value receivers for a whole tree consistently, or the same node type behaves differently depending on how it was stored.
A new struct silently satisfies nothing: the compiler cannot tell you that an evaluator no longer covers the node set, so keep an explicit default returning an error in any type switch.

variants.name: Concrete node structs with one Eval(node) type switch
variants.idiom_name: single Eval(node Node, env *Env) function type-switching on the concrete node
variants.implementation_notes: The other common Go shape, used by Monkey-style interpreters and by hashicorp/hil: nodes are plain structs behind a marker interface and a single Eval function type-switches on the concrete type. The operation belongs to the evaluator rather than the node, so adding print, check or compile passes is a sibling function; the price is that a new node type is invisible until every type switch is updated by hand.
pitfalls: The type switch is only as complete as the author's memory: a default branch that panics turns a grammar bug into a crash instead of a diagnostic.
Each operation repeats the dispatch and often the traversal; once there are three passes, the duplication is the Visitor-shaped problem this form was supposed to avoid - factor a Walk helper.
Interfaces in Go are satisfied implicitly, so a typo in a marker method makes a node compile but never match any case.
